lessonTitle: Resuscitation and Treatment Escalation Decisions: Plans, Relatives and Documentation

blocks.text: At 02:30 you are called to a frail 84-year-old woman whose breathing is getting worse. Her daughter, who has just arrived, grips your arm and asks, 'Is she dying? Are you going to do CPR?' Nobody wrote down what this patient would want, and the answer you give in the next two minutes will be remembered by the family for the rest of their lives.

blocks.markdown: A **treatment escalation plan (TEP)** is a documented, individualised plan that sets out in advance what treatments a patient should and should not receive if they deteriorate, and where they should be cared for. A decision about **cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)** is one part of a TEP, not a substitute for it. Good planning protects patients from treatments that cannot help them and from missed treatments that could. In the UK this work is guided by the law (the Mental Capacity Act 2005 in England and Wales, with different rules in Scotland and Northern Ireland), General Medical Council guidance and joint national guidance such as the Resuscitation Council UK document on decisions relating to CPR and the ReSPECT process; check the versions current in your trust.

blocks.title: DNACPR
blocks.text: A 'do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation' decision means that if the patient's heart or breathing stops, CPR will not be attempted. It applies only to CPR. It does not mean 'do not treat', and every other treatment the patient needs and would want should continue.

headers: Element of a treatment escalation plan
rows: Clinical summary
Diagnoses, frailty, prognosis and likely events
Lets the next doctor understand why the plan was made
Patient's values and preferences
What matters to the patient and what they would not accept
Keeps the plan person-centred
Capacity and who was involved
Whether the patient could take part, and the relatives, carers or attorneys consulted
Shows the decision was lawful and consultative
Clinical recommendations
The ceiling of care (for example ward-based care, higher-level monitoring, intensive care) and specific treatments to be considered or avoided
Guides emergency decisions when the patient cannot speak
CPR status
Whether CPR should be attempted, with the reason
Avoids both unwanted CPR and wrongly withheld CPR
Clinician details and review
Name, grade, date, time, signature and when the plan will be reviewed
Makes the document accountable and up to date
blocks.caption: Typical elements of a treatment escalation plan; the exact form (for example ReSPECT) is set locally.

blocks.title: Constructing a plan for a frail patient
blocks.prompt: A 79-year-old woman with severe heart failure, frailty and two recent admissions is admitted with decompensated heart failure. She has capacity and tells you she wants to avoid being kept alive on machines but would like treatment on the ward that can get her home. Outline the plan, teaching example only, to be agreed with a senior.

steps.text: Assess capacity first for this decision: she can understand, retain, weigh and communicate, so she makes the choices and her wishes lead the plan.
Record her values: she values being at home and wants to avoid prolonged organ support. Document her own words where possible.

Set the ceiling of care: ward-based treatment including intravenous diuretics, oxygen and antibiotics if needed, with senior review of any treatment that would need higher levels of care; she does not wish to be considered for intubation and intensive care.

Decide on CPR together: the senior clinician explains that CPR is unlikely to succeed in her condition and may cause harm, she agrees that CPR should not be attempted, and this is recorded as a DNACPR decision within the plan.
Record who was involved, ask whether she would like her daughter told, then give the plan a review date and ensure the form stays with her notes.

blocks.answer: A person-centred plan states: full ward-based treatment, no intensive care or intubation by the patient's choice, DNACPR agreed with her, recorded by a senior with a review date. Treatments within the ceiling still go ahead.

blocks.title: DNACPR is not 'do not treat'
blocks.text: Misreading a DNACPR form as permission to withhold antibiotics, fluids, oxygen or ward review is a common and serious error. A patient with a DNACPR decision who develops a reversible problem still deserves full assessment and treatment within the plan.

blocks.markdown: **Who decides, and who must be asked?** If the patient has capacity, the decision about treatment is theirs; clinicians must explain and recommend, and relatives cannot consent or refuse on their behalf (the patient may choose to involve them). Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision-specific and is assumed unless shown otherwise. If the patient lacks capacity, the decision-maker (usually the senior clinician) acts in the patient's best interests after consulting those close to the patient, any court-appointed deputy and any valid attorney, and after checking for a valid advance decision. In England, case law (the Tracey judgment) says there should be a presumption in favour of involving the patient in a DNACPR decision unless it would cause physical or psychological harm, and involving those close to the patient where the patient lacks capacity, unless there are good reasons not to; confirm current guidance.

headers: Notes (England and Wales, check local rules)
rows: Patient with capacity
The patient decides after discussion; relatives involved if the patient wishes
Relatives cannot override a capacitous patient
Patient lacks capacity, no attorney or advance decision
Senior clinician decides in best interests after consulting those close to the patient
Consultation seeks the patient's own views, not the relatives' preference
Valid health and welfare attorney covering life-sustaining treatment
Attorney decides within the Mental Capacity Act
Check the registered document and its scope
Valid and applicable advance decision refusing CPR
The advance decision is binding if it meets the legal criteria
Must be written, signed and witnessed for life-sustaining treatment, and applicable to the circumstances
blocks.caption: Who is involved in a CPR or escalation decision depends on capacity and legal documents.

blocks.markdown: **Communicating with relatives of a critically ill patient.** Prepare first: know the facts, the observations, the plan and the name of the senior in charge. Find a quiet space, introduce yourself and your role, and sit down. Ask what the family already understand, give a 'warning shot' that the news is serious, then use short, jargon-free sentences. Be honest about uncertainty, avoid false reassurance and do not promise what you cannot guarantee. Allow silence and emotion, acknowledge distress, and check understanding by inviting them to say it back. Confidentiality still applies: share information the patient would want shared, or what is in their best interests if they lack capacity. Use a professional interpreter rather than a relative if language is a barrier.

items: Introduce yourself and your role; confirm who you are speaking to and their relationship to the patient.
Ask what they understand and what the patient would have wanted.
Give a warning shot, then explain in plain language what is happening and what is being done.
Explain what a DNACPR or escalation decision does and does not mean, and who is responsible for the decision.
Invite questions, acknowledge emotions, and agree the next contact and who they can call.

blocks.title: Documenting a conversation with a relative
blocks.prompt: A 72-year-old man lacks capacity because of severe sepsis. At 03:10 a senior and you speak to his wife about a TEP with a DNACPR decision. Write the key items the entry must contain and say why.

steps.text: Start with date, time and place of the discussion, and list the people present: the senior doctor, the wife, the nurse and yourself, with names and roles.
Record the assessment of capacity: that the patient lacks capacity for this decision because of acute illness, and how this was assessed.

Record what was discussed: the clinical situation, the proposed plan including what treatment will continue, and the wife's account of the patient's own views, which the decision-maker takes into account.
Record the decision and the reasoning, who made it, and that the wife was informed that the decision is made in the patient's best interests rather than by her.
Record a review date and any information given, then sign with your name, grade and professional number, and make sure the form and notes are visible to the next team.

blocks.answer: The entry should be contemporaneous, dated, timed, signed, identify participants, state capacity and the reasoning, record the family's contribution and the plan, and be reviewed.

blocks.markdown: **Documenting decisions clearly and legally.** The record is the only way the next team will know what was decided. Write it at the time, in clear language free of ambiguous abbreviations, with date, time, your name, grade and signature. State the decision, the reasons, the discussion with the patient or those close to the patient, capacity, and the review plan. The form should travel with the patient and be reviewed after a change in condition. A decision not to discuss with a patient or relatives must be explained in the record. Never leave an entry that says only 'not for escalation'; say precisely which treatments are included and which are not. Follow your organisation's policy and the General Medical Council's Good medical practice.

blocks.title: What a good record shows
blocks.text: A reader who never met the patient should be able to see what was decided, why, who was involved, what the patient or relatives said, and when the plan will be reviewed. If the entry could not defend the decision to a coroner, a complaints panel or a grieving relative, it is not yet clear enough.

points: A treatment escalation plan sets ceilings of care and CPR status together, so emergency teams know what to do and why.
DNACPR applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment continues.
With capacity the patient decides; without capacity the senior acts in best interests after consulting those close to the patient, checking for valid attorneys and advance decisions.
Speak to relatives in a quiet space, in plain language, honestly, and document the conversation, the decision, the reasons and a review date.

questions.stem: Which statement about a DNACPR decision is correct?

options.text: It applies only to attempts at resuscitation and does not mean other appropriate treatment should be withheld
It applies automatically to every patient over 80 years old
It means the patient is not to be reviewed by doctors if they deteriorate
It means the patient should not be given antibiotics or intravenous fluids

questions.correctOptionText: It applies only to attempts at resuscitation and does not mean other appropriate treatment should be withheld

distractorRationale.b: Age alone must never trigger such a decision; it is individual.
distractorRationale.c: False: ongoing review and treatment continue.
distractorRationale.d: Confuses DNACPR with a ceiling of care.

questions.explanation: A DNACPR decision is limited to cardiopulmonary resuscitation and says nothing about other treatments, which are governed by the wider plan and the patient's wishes. Treating it as a general 'do not treat' instruction is a recognised cause of harm.

questions.stem: A competent adult patient has said that CPR should not be attempted. Her son disagrees and demands that it should be. The son's wishes override the patient's decision.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A patient with capacity decides about their own treatment, and relatives have no legal right to consent to or refuse treatment on their behalf. Clinicians should listen to the son's concerns and explain the reasoning, but the patient's informed decision stands.

questions.stem: Which set of items best describes the content of a treatment escalation plan?

options.text: Only the name of the nurse in charge and the ward bed number
A list of every medicine the patient has taken in the last year
A clinical summary, the patient's wishes, capacity and who was consulted, recommended levels of care including CPR status, and clinician details with a review date
Only the patient's age and whether CPR is to be attempted

questions.correctOptionText: A clinical summary, the patient's wishes, capacity and who was consulted, recommended levels of care including CPR status, and clinician details with a review date

distractorRationale.b: A drug history is not a treatment escalation plan.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: covers the standard elements of a TEP.
distractorRationale.d: Too narrow; omits levels of care, preferences and review.

questions.explanation: A plan should explain why the decision was made, what treatments would and would not be offered and how the patient or relatives took part. Date, signature and review are essential so the plan is accountable and updated.

questions.stem: A frail 77-year-old man after a hip fracture has a TEP stating: ward-based care including intravenous antibiotics, not for intensive care, DNACPR. Overnight he becomes hypotensive and febrile from a chest infection. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Ignore the plan until the morning ward round
Continue active ward-based treatment, such as oxygen, fluids and antibiotics, within the plan, and involve a senior
Withhold antibiotics and fluids because of the DNACPR decision
Transfer to intensive care despite the plan

questions.correctOptionText: Continue active ward-based treatment, such as oxygen, fluids and antibiotics, within the plan, and involve a senior

distractorRationale.a: Unsafe; the plan is meant to be used immediately.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the plan permits these treatments.
distractorRationale.c: Misapplies a DNACPR; antibiotics and fluids are within the plan.
distractorRationale.d: Contradicts the documented ceiling without new discussion.

questions.explanation: The plan sets a ceiling at ward-based care and withholds CPR and intensive care only; it expressly includes antibiotics. A new reversible problem such as infection should be treated inside the plan, and any wish to depart from it requires senior review and discussion.

questions.stem: You need to speak to the husband of a patient who has become critically ill. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Find a private space, introduce yourself, ask what he understands, give a warning shot and explain in plain language
Reassure him that everything will be fine to reduce his distress
Avoid mentioning the possibility of death to prevent upset
Talk in the corridor using medical terminology to be precise

questions.correctOptionText: Find a private space, introduce yourself, ask what he understands, give a warning shot and explain in plain language

distractorRationale.a: Correct: follows good practice for breaking serious news.

questions.explanation: A quiet setting, introductions, checking understanding and plain language give relatives the best chance to take in difficult information, and a warning shot prepares them. Honesty with compassion is expected; false reassurance and avoidance cause harm.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man lacks capacity because of sepsis. A DNACPR decision was made overnight by the on-call team. His daughter is angry that no one spoke to the family and says 'you have written him off'. Discuss how you would respond and the principles that apply.
markingGuide: Listens, acknowledges her distress and apologises that she was not involved earlier, without being defensive
Explains that DNACPR applies only to CPR and that all other appropriate treatment continues
States the legal framework: best interests, consultation with those close to the patient where practicable, and the Mental Capacity Act in England and Wales
Seeks her knowledge of the patient's own wishes and values, making clear that the decision is a clinical one made in his best interests, not hers to make
Involves a senior, reviews the decision in light of her information and offers a second opinion if she remains concerned
Documents the discussion, the decision and its review date, with time, name and signature
Avoids false promises and uses plain language with space for questions
questions.explanation: The strongest answers combine communication skill with legal accuracy: the decision is made in the patient's best interests after consultation, relatives are not the decision-makers. Marks also go for recording the discussion, the reasons and any change of plan.

questions.stem: Which entry about a DNACPR decision is the best example of clear and lawful documentation?

options.text: An initialled mark on the front of the folder
'For no escalation' without detail
Date and time, participants, capacity assessment, discussion content, the decision and reasons, review date, and signature with name and grade
'DNACPR agreed with family' with no date or signature

questions.correctOptionText: Date and time, participants, capacity assessment, discussion content, the decision and reasons, review date, and signature with name and grade

distractorRationale.a: Unclear and not contemporaneous or explained.
distractorRationale.b: Ambiguous and open to harmful interpretation.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: contains the elements needed for accountability.
distractorRationale.d: Not timed or signed; no reasoning or capacity assessment.

questions.explanation: A good record shows what was decided, why and with whom, so another clinician can understand and justify it. Missing times, signatures, reasons or capacity assessment make the entry unsafe and open to challenge.

questions.stem: A DNACPR decision that has been discussed verbally with the patient does not need to be recorded in the notes provided the patient understood.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The record is the only reliable way for other teams to know what was decided, so every decision, the reasons and the discussions must be written down, dated, timed and signed. A verbal agreement that is not recorded can be lost between shifts and may lead to unwanted or withheld CPR.

questions.stem: A patient lacks capacity and has no attorney or advance decision. The senior clinician judges that CPR would not work. The patient's wife insists CPR must be attempted. Which is the best approach?

options.text: Explore the patient's own views with her, explain the reasoning and the best-interests framework, involve a senior, offer a second opinion, and document it all
Hand the decision to the wife and follow her wishes whatever they are
Tell her nothing and complete the form quietly
Agree to attempt CPR on her say-so and avoid documenting the disagreement

questions.correctOptionText: Explore the patient's own views with her, explain the reasoning and the best-interests framework, involve a senior, offer a second opinion, and document it all

distractorRationale.a: Correct: consultation without handing the decision to the relative.
distractorRationale.b: Relatives are consulted, not the decision-makers.
distractorRationale.c: Fails the duty to involve those close to the patient unless harm would result.

questions.explanation: Those close to the patient should be asked about the patient's values and wishes, and the senior clinician then decides what is in the patient's best interests, explaining the reasons. A second opinion and clear documentation are good practice, and current national guidance should be consulted for the details of conflict.

questions.stem: Explain how a treatment escalation plan differs from a DNACPR form and why it is useful to the junior doctor called to a deteriorating patient at night.
markingGuide: DNACPR concerns only whether CPR is attempted
A TEP is broader: ceiling of care, preferred places of care and specific treatments to consider or avoid
Includes patient's values and preferences, capacity and who was involved
Includes clinical summary and review date and clinician signature
Helps the junior act quickly and appropriately, for example starting ward-based treatment or knowing that intensive care is not planned, and knowing when to call a senior
Prevents both overtreatment and wrongly withheld treatment
questions.explanation: A TEP gives the on-call doctor a documented, person-centred roadmap beyond a single CPR decision, so appropriate treatments proceed and inappropriate ones are avoided. Credit goes for naming its elements and giving a concrete way it helps out of hours.
